short_explanation: Living, finite and renewable resources are grouped as available inputs, while the conditions that sustain or renew them remain outside the system boundary.
Resource availability is represented without ecological health, regeneration rate or habitat condition directly governing whether extraction should occur.
Rights to access and remove resources can be clearer than the responsibilities to maintain the ecology from which they originate.
Material is taken from an ecology, but the diagram does not yet require a reciprocal return of care, nutrients, habitat or regenerative capacity.
Land disturbance, habitat disruption, water effects and local pollution can occur outside the material quantity carried into the next stage.
Industrial demand can operate faster than mineral formation, forest succession, soil development or ecological recovery.
Processing standardises matter into predictable feedstocks, often removing traces of origin, prior use and ecological context.
Feedback may optimise temperature, chemistry or yield inside the process while wider exchanges with water, organisms, soils and habitats remain excluded.
Residues, heat, emissions and contaminated water can leave the useful material stream without becoming accountable relationships within the design system.
A predefined form and performance state is imposed on matter so that variation is reduced and the product can be repeated.
A controller may exchange information with a responsive material, but wider exchanges with ecological systems are commonly removed from the feedback loop.
Material variability and environmental change are often treated as deviations to correct rather than conditions through which the system might evolve.
Products are commonly stabilised around a finished state, limiting their ability to continue changing with use, environment and ecological succession.
The places of extraction, manufacture, use and disposal can be geographically separated, making ecological and social consequences difficult to perceive together.
Standardised logistics can treat materials as equivalent units in motion while their local ecological origins and destination conditions disappear.
Transport energy, infrastructure and emissions support every stage but are often treated as secondary to the object being produced.
The product is treated as finished when it enters use, even though users, environments and material conditions continue to change.

annotation_class: Repair, care and adaptation are frequently less visible than replacement, allowing functional value to be discarded before material value is exhausted.
Use may generate performance data, but the source ecology and wider resource cycles rarely influence how the product behaves or how long it remains in service.
Products and components may remain idle or be discarded because systems for shared use, transfer and collective stewardship are weak.

short_explanation: A product reaches End of Use through a human decision or waste category, rather than through the ecological completion of a life cycle.
Once function or ownership ends, remaining form, components and material knowledge can be collapsed into a lower-value waste stream.
Manufactured materials rarely redistribute safely into soils, organisms and nutrient cycles in the way accumulated biological matter can after death.
Responsibility can pass between user, collector, exporter, recycler and disposal operator, obscuring who remains accountable for the material.
Reuse preserves more existing form and embodied work than recycling, but it usually appears only after the primary ownership and use system has ended.
A reusable product or component only remains in circulation where systems exist to inspect, transfer, adapt and make it available to another user.
Keeping an object in human use can delay extraction and waste, but it does not by itself reconnect the material with the ecology from which it originated.
Recycling usually returns matter to industrial processing rather than restoring it to the ecological source or cycle from which it was taken.
Reprocessing often destroys the form, assembly and functional relationships already created, retaining material while losing higher levels of value.
Collection, sorting, cleaning, transport and transformation require additional energy and can generate emissions, residues and material losses.
A material may remain in circulation while moving into a lower-grade function that cannot replace the original material or product.
